content.title: Thanks to reviewer ZsuU
content.comment:
we added visual demos for zoomed-in single intersections to better compare different methods of traffic light control logic. The conclusion is: Our GESA could release the traffic jam most promptly and efficiently, even if all the selected intersections are the busiest ones in the corresponding scenarios. The single intersection demos have been uploaded to our GitHub repo: https://github.com/AnonymousIDforSubmission/GESA

The detailed results are given as below, with their following shortcut links:

(1) Arterial 4x4: https://imgur.com/a/7pvvpzD
As shown in the demo, the Arterial 4x4 has quite high traffic volume, especially in the selected intersection: both FTC and GESA-Single get quite long traffic queues in the West and South entering approaches, and FTC also has a long queue in the North approach. However, our GESA could promptly and dynamically release the traffic jam.

(2) Cologne 8: https://imgur.com/a/GtDciQq
As shown in the demo, the North entering approach has quite high traffic inflow, and all the benchmarks could not release the flow on time, resulting in a long queue. Our GESA could release the jam timely.

(3) Fenglin: https://imgur.com/a/dKB6Blk
As mentioned in the paper, Fenglin is a corridor with an East-West main road. As shown in the demo, high volume of traffic flow concentrated in the middle through-lane of the East entering approach, resulting in the traffic jam in the benchmark methods. MaxPressure and GESA have fewer jams than MPLight in that lane, and GESA has fewer accumulated vehicles on other lanes.

Please accept our sincere thanks again for all your suggestions on our work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer rkV5 (Part 3/3)
content.comment:
> "Technical Novelty And Significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
Empirical Novelty And Significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel."

**Response**: Regarding the contributions of our work, we give our response to this question in Point 1 in the General Response. Please allow us to reply the same here: 

We would like first to emphasize and clarify the **motivation and contribution** of our GESA model: To the best of our knowledge, the biggest limitation of all the existing works is: they still face tremendous challenges to jumping out from the simulation systems (e.g., SUMO) and to be deployed in the real cities. This is known as *sim2real* challenge. The challenge mainly comes from the wide gap between the real complex cities and the simplified simulation systems, as we mentioned on Page 2, Paragraph 3 about the different combinations of movements and approaches within an intersection. The solution we offer is the higher model generalization, such that we could significantly narrow the gap between the simulation and the real world. Our model is designed exactly this way: we achieve higher generalization by co-training multiple scenarios. To enable co-training, we design a general plug-in module to standardize all different intersections from various multiple scenarios; we design a unified state and action space; and we use A3C to train the multiple scenarios simultaneously; and we build real scenarios where we exactly plan to implement our model in the future. All these lead us closer to achieving the ultimate goal: **to deploy RL-based TSC in real cities**.

Our model’s improved generalization is further proved after we recently succeeded in reproducing the result of MetaLight in SUMO, which could also co-train multi-scenarios based on Meta Reinforcement Learning. The results have been updated in Table 1 on Page 8 (a shortcut and anonymous link to view our result:  https://i.imgur.com/knRTklg.png). As we could observe, our GESA still beats MetaLight in four scenarios, with **+14.38%** improvement on average. This might be because Metalight is designed to be trained with two scenarios only each time and the scenarios that MetaLight used are homogeneous, resulting in limited generalization and an unstable valuation (shown in Fig. 12(a), shortcut link https://i.imgur.com/NY4TRVJ.jpg). However, MetaLight beats GESA in the *Arterial 4×4* by a small margin of 3.43%. This may be because, for some scenarios, there are conflicts between the sub-rewards, making it difficult for GESA to promote them in all the scenarios simultaneously. The results are also provided in a plot format Fig. 11(https://i.imgur.com/VHgG9lQ.png) in Appendix D.1 on Page 16. From this figure, one can intuitively check out the performance comparison between our model and benchmarks.

Given our model further narrows the gap between simulation and real-world implementation, as well as considering that Reviewers 1 and 2 have all acknowledged that our work has good merits, we believe our model is worth sharing with the community. In the future, we plan to deploy the GESA model in real cities.

content.title: Response to Reviewer rkV5 (Part 2/3)
content.comment:
> **Comment 3**: "The paper needs more experiment results and metrics to support the model performance. Like doing a melt-down experiment/sensitive analysis to figure out the contributions of each part of the model."

**Response**: Thanks for your constructive suggestions. In Appendix, we conduct additional ablation studies in terms of the model components, rewards, and the number of co-trained scenarios. Furthermore, the analysis is provided why the results from multiple scenarios is better than the ones from a single scenario. We also attach some visualized demonstrations of the simulation in the supplementary materials and more on the GitHub page.

In summary, through the experiments, the following findings can be concluded: (1) our algorithm achieves higher performance and stability than metalight, a state of the art baseline; (2) multiple sub-rewards works better than a single one; (3) multi-scenario co-training can overcome the local optimum problem which few-scenario training tends to fall into.

For more details, please refer to Appendix D and E on pages 15~19.

We also summarize all the ablation studies we have done as below:

In the appendix: 
- Added more **experiment results** in Appendix.D, with the reward comparison in a figure format (Fig.11 https://i.imgur.com/VHgG9lQ.png), and evaluation plot (Fig.12 https://i.imgur.com/NY4TRVJ.jpg) for MetaLight and GESA.
- Added prudent **ablation studies**
  1.  Ablation on the **model components** (Appendix.E.1 on Page 16), showing the importance of the A3C module (GESA-sequential-train is not improving the reward, as shown in Fig.12(b), https://i.imgur.com/NY4TRVJ.jpg). 
  2. Ablation on **rewards**, showing multi-rewards is better than single reward (Table 4, Appendix.E.2 on Page 17, https://i.imgur.com/X7XkGgG.jpg)
  3.  Ablation of the impact of **the number of co-trained scenarios**, showing more scenarios gives more improvement (Table 5, Appendix.E.3.1 on Page 18, https://i.imgur.com/Xdh1Nck.png)
  4.  Analyzed the **reason** why the result of multiple scenarios is better than that of a single scenario, which all reviewers are most concerned about: our conclusion is training in a single scenario may lead to a local optimum. For example, in Fig. 13 (https://i.imgur.com/8TzhCQ9.png), the GESA-single gets stuck in a local optimum where going-straight is over-prioritized to be released first (see Appendix.E.3.2 on Pages 18-19).
- Add four **demos** in the supplementary material, more demos and code can be found on the anonymous Github page in the paper: https://github.com/AnonymousIDforSubmission/GESA. We also visualize some demos in Appendix.F, Pages 19 and 20, for example in Fig. 14 (https://i.imgur.com/hqCoeCz.jpg) and Fig. 15 (https://i.imgur.com/EaaSmik.jpg), at the same time stamp, our GESA model achieves least congestion.

content.title: Response to Reviewer rkV5 (Part 1/3)
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer rkV5 for reviewing our paper and providing helpful feedback on our work. We address all of Reviewer rkV5’s concerns and the responses to the comments are listed below.

> **Comment 1**: "The model couldn’t generate the scenarios in more complex conditions, like the intersections with more than four approaches"

**Response**: Thanks for the concerns. : We give our response to this question in the Point 2 in the General Response. Please allow us to reply the same here: 

In the experiment, our model is designed to be more applicable to intersections with no more than four approaches. It should be noted that it is a demonstration, and the threshold "four" is not fixed, that is, intersections with five, six, or even more approaches can also be treated following the similar pipeline. When the threshold is enlarged, one needs to:
1. modify the angles interval in Algorithm 1, 
2. update the conflict matrix of movements (in Fig. 2.(b), https://i.imgur.com/KbgKTKF.png) and available phases, for instance, the conflict matrix will be extended to a 10 × 10 conflict matrix if 10 phases are available 
3. enlarge the model output (i.e., action space) to 10 available phases.

The reasons why we choose "four" are: 
1. For the intersections in real-world road networks, two-approach, three-approach, and four-approach ones occupy dominant proportions. Intersections with more than four approaches account for less than 5%.
2. According to our practical statistics in Nanshan and Fenglin districts, 
there are no intersections with more than four entering approaches, so setting "four" in the proposed GPI module is quite enough to handle the realistic scenarios. 

Overall, the >4-approach intersections or > 8 available phases are relatively rare, and the design for such intersections in the GPI module is not worth the cost. If needed, we will consider extending the GPI module to handle such situations specifically in our future work.

Moreover, one may be confused with the terms "legs" and "approaches" for an intersection. For example, a six-legged intersection can still have only four entering approaches, as shown in Fig. 16 (https://i.imgur.com/YbCvv5a.png). The rest two legs are exiting approaches without the need for signal control.

> **Comment 2**: "The paper didn’t provide the code and dataset for reviewing."

**Response**: Sorry for our negligence. We have uploaded our source code, simulation scenarios, and visualized demonstrations to the anonymous GitHub page https://github.com/AnonymousIDforSubmission/GESA as well as the supplementary materials for reviewing and easy reproduction.

> **Comment 2**: "I would like to see additional ablation on the reward function design."

**Response**: We make an ablation on the reward function design in the revision. We conduct a single-component v.s. all-component reward ablation experiment in the co-training setting, the results are shown in Table 4 (Appendix E.2, Page 17, https://i.imgur.com/X7XkGgG.jpg). 

It can be seen that even though the GESA trained with a single component may outperform under the particular metric, its performance on the remaining metrics is unremarkable. For example, in the *Ingolstadt 21* scenario, GESA's wait time achieves the best on the wait time metric, but degrades about 150.5%, 1522.4%, and 1577.1% on the delay time, queue length, and pressure compared to the canonical GESA, respectively. The higher delay time and lower wait time indicate that the vehicles move slower even though stop infrequently, and there is a higher potential for jams accordingly.

> **Comment 5**: "Section 5 - missing qualitative comparison between the baseline strategies vs. policy discovered by the model."

**Response**: We have added the visualization as .gif files in the supplementary material, and you can find more visualization results on our anonymous GitHub page: https://github.com/AnonymousIDforSubmission/GESA.

In Appendix F on Pages 19-20, we also present the visualization.

Fig. 14 (https://i.imgur.com/hqCoeCz.jpg) shows the 318-th simulation step in the Arterial 4x4 scenario. Due to the high traffic volume, longer queues are formed in several intersections when the traffic is controlled by the FTC method (Fig. 14.(a)). The GESA-Single model (Fig. 14.(b)) can alleviate the condition to some extent, while our GESA model (Fig. 14.\(c\)) shortens the queue length significantly, which demonstrates its superiority intuitively.

In the Fenglin scenario in Fig. 15 (https://i.imgur.com/EaaSmik.jpg), we could observe the same: congestions happen the worst in the MaxPressure and MPLight since the traffic flow is generated based on the real-world peak hour.



> **Comment 6**: "section 5.1 - "its traffic flow data is simulated based on the actual flow" the authors should specify maybe in an appendix where this data come from?"

**Response**: For each intersection, live cameras are deployed to count the passing vehicles and calculate the average traffic flow. (1) We select the peak hour in the red box in Fig. 10c (https://i.imgur.com/ylkPC2S.jpg), and inject the flow from the boundary intersection into the network; (2) The turn ratio in each intersection also needs to be defined. We calculate it based on the real data for each entering approach. For example, the ratio of through:right:left for an intersection is 5:3:2, then the traffic volume is split as 5:3:2; (3) Lastly, we place 50-meter Lane-Area (E2) detectors in each entering lane to get the observations such as queue length and occupancy, and we place Multi-Entry-Exit Detectors (E3) between the entry and exit to get the delay time and wait time.

For more details about the Fenglin flow and how to build the two real-world scenarios, please refer to Appendix C.2 on Page 14. 

> **Comment 7**: "table 1 - how do the authors explain that GESA multi-scenario outperforms GESA single-scenario for a few of the environments?"

**Response**: We will answer this question with one experiment first. We did an extra ablation study on the different amounts of co-training scenarios. As shown in Table 5 (https://i.imgur.com/Xdh1Nck.png), it can be observed that the reward increases monotonically as the number of co-training scenarios rising. This means that adding more scenarios can facilitate the model performance, and the proposed general scenario-agnostic method works very well. This may be because the different scenarios may share similar latent spatiotemporal correlation, and co-training achieves the effect of 1+1>2 by leveraging this spatiotemporal correlation. More results are in Appendix E.3.1 on Page 18.


Now we come back to your question in a more specific way. Through visualization in Fig. 13 (https://i.imgur.com/8TzhCQ9.png), we find that single-scenario training is prone to falling into local optima than large-scale co-training. For example, *Fenglin* road network is a corridor; thus, an obvious issue of the single-training one is that its left-turn traffic movement has a lower priority of release than going straight, resulting in more queue length and pressure in the left lanes. This is because *Fenglin* road network is a corridor that has an East-West main road and multiple North-South branch roads. Vehicles spend much more time on the main road than on branch roads; therefore, it is easier for the agent to learn that the priority of letting go straight is higher than turning left. Once the agent is over-optimized in taking going straight action, it is difficult to break out because it will get smaller rewards for exploration over a long time.


This reason can also explain why the improvement of multi-scenario performance is trivial compared to the one in Grid 4×4, the single scenario. The road network of the Grid 4×4 scenario is symmetrical, and the distribution of traffic flow is smooth and relatively uniform. While in Arterial 4×4, even if its road network is very symmetrical, its traffic flow distribution is very uneven, the top and tail row intersections have heavy traffic flow, and two middle row intersections have no traffic flow in East-West lanes.

For more details about why multi-scenario outperforms single-scenario, please refer to Appendix E.3.2 on Pages 18 and 19, you can also find visualizations of single training and co-training in *Fenglin* scenario.

content.comment:
> **Comment 2**: "algorithm 1 - For a crooked kind of Y-shaped intersection, selecting either of the top branches of the Y as north would cause algorithm 1 to fail, but selecting the bottom branch as north would result in success. The authors are filtering out intersections that they don't need to if they randomly select north. An easy fix would be to attempt algorithm 1 on all possible choices of North until one of them passes, and fail only if it never passes."

**Response**: Thanks for your great idea. Algorithm 1 will indeed tend to fail if the choice of North is unsuitable for Y-shaped intersections. This is a helpful improvement of our Algorithm 1, and we have added the iterations into the revision.

> **Comment 3**: "section 4.3 - the authors should include a formal definition of queue length, wait time, delay time, and pressure. They should also specify the value of the weights that they use in the reward function."

**Response**: Sorry for missing the corresponding descriptions. In the revision, we declare them in Appendix A on Page 12. The definitions of our sub-rewards are also listed as follows:

 - **Delay Time** $T^d_i$: The delay time for the intersection $i$ is the average of all the lanes' delay time. The delay time for a lane is the sum of all vehicles' delay time on the lane. A vehicle delay time $d_\textit{v}$ is calculated by: 
$$
d_\textit{v} = \Delta t \left ( 1 - \frac{v_\textit{v}(t)}{v_{max}} \right )
$$
where $\Delta t$ is interval time, $v_\textit{v}(t)$ is the average speed over the interval time, and $v_{max}$ is the max speed of vehicle $\textit{v}$.   Its unit is second (s).

 - **Wait Time** $T^w_i$: The wait time for the intersection $i$ is the average of all the lanes it contains, whereas the wait time for a particular lane is the sum of all vehicles' stop time on it. The unit is second $(s)$.

- **Queue Length** $L_i$: The queue length is defined as the average of all-lanes vehicle queue length in an intersection, which is in meter $(m)$.

- **Pressure** $P_i$: The pressure of the intersection $i$ is the difference between the queuing vehicles numbers on entering and exiting approaches. Intuitively, a higher pressure indicates a greater imbalance between the entering and exiting lanes.

For more details, please refer to Appendix A on Page 12. 

The smaller the four reward components are, the better the traffic condition is. To maximize the total reward, the weights are set to negative:  $w_{\textit{delay time}} = -1e^{-5}, w_{\textit{wait time}} = -1e^{-3}, w_{\textit{queue length}} = -1e^{-3}, w_{\textit{pressure}} = -5e^{-3}$. 

The re-scale weights $w_*$ are designed to balance each component in the reward. In our experiment, we decided the weights according to parameter tuning so that the four reward components are on a similar scale. Without balancing the four components, the training will be led to one direction that only maximizes the most dominant reward component.

> **Comment 4**: "tables 1 and 2 - the authors should report delay time, wait time, queue length, and pressure in interpretable units. Are delay time and wait time measured in seconds? I recommend the authors report these numbers as positive numbers and in a plot format instead of a table."

**Response**: Thanks for your valuable suggestions. We update all the values in tables and restore the positive sub-rewards under interpretable units. Please refer to the tables for review. For instance, as shown in Table 1 (https://i.imgur.com/knRTklg.png).


It is worth mentioning that we also reproduce the MetaLight, another multi-scenario model based on Meta Reinforcement Learning. 

The results are also provided in a plot format (Fig.11 https://i.imgur.com/VHgG9lQ.png) in Appendix D.1 on Page 16, due to the limited space in the main text. From this figure, one can intuitively check out the performance comparison between our model and benchmarks.

content.comment:
Before we give our response point-to-point, we would like to thank Reviewer bTdE for his/her detailed comments and helpful feedback on our work. We address all of Reviewer bTdE’s suggestions, and we add a 9-page long appendix with detailed information about what you are concerned about, including reward definitions, scenario introductions, prudent ablation studies, qualitative visual demos, and more! We respond to the specific comments below.

> **Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility:** " I think it still might be important to fine-tune a traffic light controller on an intersection individually, but a "universal" parametric traffic light controller should provide a good initialization."

**Response**:  Exactly like what you mentioned, the model generalization is also extended in the setting when we try to transfer our GESA from one region to another, and from one city to another, our GESA could do a better and lighter transfer, namely a better initialization without heavy manual labeling. As you suggested, a fine-tuning step afterward undoubtedly will further guarantee the performance of each intersection.

However, this "initialization" is better to be obtained with multi-scenarios co-trained by our GESA. As mentioned in Point 3 in the General Response, individual-scenario-training has the risk of falling into a local optimum, resulting in an ill performance like what happened in *Fenglin*.

> **Comment 1.1**: "definition 4 - Could the authors comment on why they don't allow the policy to learn the phases?"

**Response**: We would like to reply to this comment from three aspects: (1) only eight feasible phases due to the conflict matrix, (2) two popular TSC systems in real industry, and (3) the complexity of action space.

(1) As shown in Fig. 2(a) (https://i.imgur.com/KbgKTKF.png), there could be conflicts between two movements. After getting the whole conflict matrix, as shown in Fig. 2(b), we could find out only 8 available phases. So, how different movements are combined for a phase is not actually learnable since there is such a conflict matrix and the feasible region for phases is thus eight. We apologize that the conflict matrix was in the first submission, and now Figure 2 is updated.


(2) There are two types of systems for TSC: (a) one is to learn the phase's cycle length and the green light ratio, whereas the phase order is fixed. This is popular in traditional systems such as SCAT and SCOOT, developed 70 years ago. (b) another is to learn how to choose the next phase (i.e., to learn phase order), whereas the phase length is fixed. The first type is based on classic transport engineering methods with analytic solutions, and the second type is more recent, flexible, and of high potential for embedding RL models into it.

(3) Why can't RL be embedded into the first type system? The reason is that: The action space will be too large to be explored since the phase cycle length and green ratio are continuous. For example, the phase cycle length could vary from 70 seconds to 180 seconds.

> **Comment 1.2**: "My sense is that the pre-processing step in algorithm 1 would filter out many real-world intersections, which seriously limits the scope of the authors' method."

**Response**: Thank you for this question. (1) If you mean that our Algo. 1 will filter out the intersections with more than four approaches, we give a summarized response towards it in Point 2 in the General Response. Please refer to there. Thank you! A quick recap is: The intersections with more than four approaches are quite niche and uncommon (accounting for 5% only). Besides, we demonstrate Algo. 1 by using a four-approach intersection as an example, it could be extended to more cases easily when we adjust the angle and conflict matrix, as mentioned before. (2) If you mean that our Algo.1 may still miss common intersections, so far after we revised Algo. 1 according to your suggestion, Algo. 1 could cover all the intersections in our seven scenarios. 

In case of some strange intersections that are hard for Algo. 1 to cover, we believe such instances are not critical, as the objective is to unify the helpful intersections for training as many as possible instead of all the intersections. Thus, the filtered-out intersections may influence the performance of the RL model but do not play a decisive role in the multi-scenario training as long as the model works on the remaining intersections. When transferring to an unseen intersection, one can manually specify the directions of the approaches for deploying the well-trained model.

content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful insights and constructive suggestions for our manuscript. We have modified the manuscript according to the invaluable comments of reviewers and highlighted the key changes in blue. Additionally, in response to the concerns, we attach the appendix at the end of the manuscript, which provides experimental details and further results. We hope these modifications can meet with approval.

**1. Motivation and Contribution**

We would like to thank the several reviewers for showing their positive recognition of our work's contribution and novelty.  We would like to take this opportunity to emphasize and clarify the **motivation and contribution** of our GESA model again: To the best of our knowledge, the biggest limitation of all the existing works is: they still face tremendous challenges to jump out from the simulation systems (e.g., SUMO) and to be deployed in the real cities. This is known as the *sim2real* challenge. The challenge mainly comes from the wide gap between the real complex cities and the simplified simulation systems, as we mentioned on Page 2, Paragraph 3, about the different combinations of movements and approaches within an intersection. The solution we offer is the higher model generalization, such that we could significantly narrow the gap between the simulation and the real world. Our model is designed exactly this way: we achieve higher generalization by co-training multiple scenarios. To enable co-training, we design a general plug-in module to standardize all different intersections from various multiple scenarios; we design a unified state and action space; and we use A3C to train the multiple scenarios simultaneously; and we build real scenarios where we exactly plan to implement our model in the future. All these lead us closer to achieving the ultimate goal: **to deploy RL-based TSC in real cities**.

Our model’s improved generalization is further proved after we recently succeeded in reproducing the result of MetaLight in SUMO, which could also co-train multi-scenarios based on Meta Reinforcement Learning. The results have been updated in Table 1 on Page 8 (a shortcut and anonymous link to view our result:  https://i.imgur.com/knRTklg.png). As we could observe, our GESA still beats MetaLight in four scenarios, with a **+14.38%** improvement on average. This might be because Metalight is designed to be trained with two scenarios only each time and the scenarios that MetaLight used are homogeneous, resulting in limited generalization and an unstable valuation (shown in Fig. 12(a), shortcut link https://i.imgur.com/NY4TRVJ.jpg). However, MetaLight beats GESA in the *Arterial 4×4* by a small margin of 3.43%. This may be because, for some scenarios, there are conflicts between the sub-rewards, making it difficult for GESA to promote them in all the scenarios simultaneously. 

The results are also provided in a plot format Fig. 11(https://i.imgur.com/VHgG9lQ.png) in Appendix D.1 on Page 16 due to the limited space in the main text. From this figure, one can intuitively check out the performance comparison between our model and benchmarks.

Our model further narrows the gap between simulation and real-world implementation. In the future, we plan to deploy the GESA model in real cities.

The authors propose to first convert intersections to a standard format, then feed traffic information through a neural network that outputs a distribution over one of eight traffic phases every 10 seconds. The authors show that after training on 6 maps, the model can control traffic on a 7th map better than baselines by 10% on average across multiple metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I found this paper well-written and interesting to read. The method is very principled; if we can train a universal traffic controller, that can make it significantly easier to apply that model in new intersections or update the model when an intersection changes. The problem fits perfectly into the reinforcement learning framework.

I do think however that the paper's empirical analysis is somewhat weak. I'm also not entirely clear on the definitions of some of the metrics that the authors use which I think would be well-suited for a section in the appendix. I will be willing to increase my score if the authors can address my questions and comments below:

- definition 4 - Could the authors comment on why they don't allow the policy to learn the phases? My sense is that the pre-processing step in algorithm 1 would filter out many real-world intersections which seriously limits the scope of the authors' method.

The authors are filtering out intersections that they don't need to if they randomly select north. An easy fix would be to attempt algorithm 1 on all possible choices of north until one of them passes, and fail only if it never passes.

- section 4.3 - the authors should include a formal definition of queue length, wait time, delay time, and pressure. They should also specify the value of the weights that they use in the reward function.

- Section 5 - missing qualitative comparison between the baseline strategies vs. policy discovered by the model. A visual is necessary for understanding if the policy would transfer to the real world, since SUMO isn't a perfect simulator so I could imagine RL discovering optimal strategies that would not work in practice. For good examples of visuals, see for instance https://mit-wu-lab.github.io/automatic_vehicular_control/ or https://fidler-lab.github.io/social-driving/

content.title: A GENERAL SCENARIO-AGNOSTIC REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FOR TRAFFIC SIGNAL CONTROL
content.abstract: Reinforcement learning has been recently adopted to revolutionize and optimize traditional traffic signal control systems. Existing methods are either based on a single scenario or multiple independent scenarios, where each scenario has a separate simulation environment with predefined road network topology and traffic signal settings. These models implement training and testing in the same scenario, thus being strictly tied up with the specific setting and sacrificing model generalization heavily. While a few recent models could be trained by multiple scenarios, they require a huge amount of manual labor to label the intersection structure, hindering the model’s generalization. In this work, we aim at a general framework that could eliminate heavy labeling and model a variety of scenarios simultaneously. To this end, we propose a GEneral Scenario-Agnostic (GESA) reinforcement learning framework for traffic signal control with: (1) A general plug-in module to map all different intersections into a unified structure, freeing us from the heavy manual labor to specify the structure of intersections; (2) A unified state and action space to keep the model input and output consistently structured; (3) A large-scale co-training with multiple scenarios, leading to a generic traffic signal control algorithm. In experiments, we demonstrate our algorithm as the first one that can be co-trained with seven different scenarios without manual annotation, and get 17.20% higher rewards than benchmarks. When dealing with a new scenario, our model can still achieve 10.36% higher rewards. The code and scenarios will be released upon acceptance.
